ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** Both sections argue that a single LLM call is brittle, hard to debug, and unreliable for complex tasks, and both preview the same four upcoming patterns. The generated section doesn't use the expected section's 'black box' metaphor specifically, but the substantive claim -- over-reliance on one call produces an unreliable, hard-to-maintain system -- is present.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** This is the most complete match of this section found across all articles graded under this guideline: all five expected points (debugging difficulty, lack of modularity, lost-in-the-middle with an explicit Lesson-3 callback, token consumption, and reliability degradation with the 98.7%-to-85% statistic) are present as explicit, individually-labeled bullets, and the added 'even minor changes to output format can cause a sharp drop in accuracy' point substantially covers the expected section's phrasing/format-sensitivity idea, which in every other article graded had no counterpart at all. Only the context-overflow/truncation point remains without a clear standalone match, which alone is treated as tolerable compression.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** All four of the guideline's clearly-named benefits are present (modularity, accuracy, debugging, flexibility with the cheap/expensive-model example). Two downsides are explicit (cost/latency, context degradation/error propagation); the distinct 'instructions lose their meaning when split' point and the 'glue code' maintenance-burden point have no separate counterpart, treated as tolerable compression consistent with every other article graded.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections build the identical 3-step chain, combine it into a sequential_workflow function, measure the same 22.20-second execution time, and reach the same conclusion about needing a faster solution. The added AppFolio case-study reference and the Pydantic-validation best practice are proportionate, on-topic additions.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections explain the independence of answering/sourcing, build the same async function pair and asyncio.gather-based parallel_workflow, report the same 22.20s-to-8.98s speedup, and cover the sequential-vs-parallel trade-off and the rate-limit caveat (backoff with jitter) with a level of detail matching the expected section.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**1:** The core ideas -- fixed workflows can't adapt, an LLM call as classifier, divide-and-conquer, and a customer-service illustration -- are all present. The expected section's model-routing callout is satisfied by the cascading-pattern mention ('a cheaper model handles simple queries and escalates complex ones to a more powerful model').

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections implement the identical IntentEnum/UserIntent classification model, the same classify_intent function, the same three specialized prompts, and the same handle_query router. As with every other article graded under this guideline, the expected section's paragraph on intent-classification best practices (taxonomy design, high-quality examples for edge cases, a two-stage retrieve-then-classify architecture) has no counterpart -- the added confidence-threshold fallback content is genuinely valuable (see DepthEnhancement below) but addresses a different question, so CoreContent still fails on that specific missing idea cluster.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**0:** Both sections define the orchestrator-worker pattern identically and frame its dynamic-nature advantage over parallelization the same way, and both walk through the same three-issue customer query with matching schemas and full working code. This section's 'this isn't free' discussion (added complexity, latency, and over-engineering risk, plus a comment that the orchestration logic itself is a real challenge) is more developed than in most articles graded, but per standing ruling it still omits a specific real-world limitation the expected section's implementation-challenges content calls for: API rate limiting. This pattern dispatches multiple LLM calls per query (orchestrator, each worker, synthesizer), making it exactly the kind of multi-call workflow this limitation applies to, and none of this section's cited challenges substitute for a dedicated treatment of it. Retroactively corrected from an earlier pass, which treated the broader complexity/latency discussion as adequate -- this is a confirmed omission, so CoreContent fails.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns, paired with matching benefits, and close by connecting the lesson to the broader practice of AI engineering and previewing what's next. The next-lesson preview covers the same theme (tools/function calling) without a specific lesson number, which per established precedent is a guideline_adherence matter, not a CoreContent one.
